Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: New costlier iPhones may boost refurbished smartphones' demand
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Apple's latest iPhone launch could trigger a fresh wave of trade-ins, while strengthening demand for older, refurbished models, as sharply higher flagship prices push buyers towards more affordable ways of entering the company's ecosystem, according to Cashify.The refurbished-device platform expects buybacks to increase within 30 days of the launch and gather pace over the following 60-90 days as supplies improve, festive offers expand and more customers upgrade.The iPhone 15 and iPhone 16 series are expected to record the strongest increase in buybacks. The iPhone 13 and 14 could continue contributing substantial volumes because of their larger installed base.Apple accounted for 65.3% of refurbished smartphone sales on its platform in 2025 and 32.6% of all devices bought back. The iPhone 13 was both its bestselling refurbished iPhone and most frequently traded-in model. The iPhone 13 represented 6.93% of Cashify's smartphone buybacks but accounted for 15.5% of refurbished demand, indicating that demand exceeded the volume volume entering its resale system.Meanwhile, refurbished-phone retailers expect demand for older iPhones to strengthen following the latest price increases, particularly among customers who want an Apple device but are unwilling to spend close to Rs 1 lakh on a new base model.Retailers also expect warranties, battery health and device certification to become more important as first-time buyers move towards the secondary market.Higher supplies would ordinarily reduce prices of outgoing models. However, Cashify expects the elevated prices of new iPhones to simultaneously lift demand for previous generations, potentially limiting the correction. Prices could therefore soften gradually instead of declining sharply.Demand is expected to shift progressively towards the iPhone 14 and 15 as availability improves, while the iPhone 16 may initially remain in the premium refurbished category because of its higher residual value.
Article Summary: Apple accounted for 65.3% of refurbished smartphone sales on Cashify's platform in 2025. The iPhone 13 was both its bestselling refurbished iPhone and most frequently traded-in model. Cashify expects the elevated prices of new iPhones to simultaneously lift demand for previous generations, potentially limiting the correction.

Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.

Article Title: Cybersecurity company warns of WhatsApp scam 'spreading fast'; says hackers using the app to distribute malicious files disguised as routine documents
Article Text:
Cybersecurity company warns of WhatsApp scam 'spreading fast'

Study found hackers using WhatsApp to distribute malicious files

How the campaign works

What WhatsApp users must do to avoid falling victims

Quick Heal Technologies Limited has issued a warning on an ongoing WhatsApp-based malware campaign targeting finance teams, senior executives, chartered accountants and individual business users. According to the cybersecurity firm, the campaign spreads through compromised WhatsApp accounts and is evolving rapidly, with attackers adopting new file formats and evasion methods to bypass security controls and establish persistent access to victims’ devices.The company cites an investigation conducted by its researchers at Seqrite Labs. The study shows that the campaign relies on trust rather than unsolicited messages from unknown numbers. Once a WhatsApp account is compromised, attackers use it to forward malicious files to the account holder’s existing contacts. Because the messages appear to come from a known colleague, client, friend or business associate, recipients may be more likely to open the attachment without independently verifying it.As per the study, the attackers are using finance- and compliance-themed filenames to create urgency and familiarity.Malicious attachments have been disguised as routine business documents, including “Financial Report,” “Account Statement,” “Outstanding Payment List” and “Debt Confirmation.” Some variants also impersonate urgent communications from regulatory institutions, including the Reserve Bank of India and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, in an effort to pressure recipients into opening the files immediately.The campaign evolves through several delivery methods. It initially spreads through malicious Visual Basic Script files, or .vbs files, sent directly through WhatsApp. The attackers later shifted to ZIP archives carrying an executable and a supporting malicious file, using DLL sideloading to make a legitimate-looking program load harmful code. The company cautions that .img and .vhd files are not ordinary photographs or documents.When a user double-clicks one of these files, Windows treats it like a newly connected disk drive, potentially exposing an executable and concealed malicious components. Users should treat an unexpected .img or .vhd attachment with the same caution they would apply to an unknown .exe file.Infected systems can use an active WhatsApp Web session to automatically forward the malicious file to the victim’s contacts, allowing the campaign to propagate further through trusted social and professional networks. The self-propagating feature expands the risk from an individual compromise into a wider business and supply-chain concern, particularly where employees, vendors, customers and finance functions communicate frequently over WhatsApp.Quick Heal Technologies Limited recommends that organisations and individuals never open an unexpected file received on WhatsApp or any messaging platform, even if it appears to come from a known contact. Recipients should verify the attachment through a separate channel, such as a phone call, rather than replying in the same conversation. Users should also routinely review WhatsApp’s Linked Devices settings and log out of web or desktop sessions they do not recognise or no longer use.The company also advises organisations to maintain updated endpoint protection, prohibit unauthorised remote-access software, monitor for suspicious driver installations and alert employees to the risks posed by finance-themed attachments and pressure-based messages. If a compromise is suspected, users should immediately log out of WhatsApp-linked devices, disconnect the affected device from the network, inform their IT or security team, and warn their contacts not to open files sent from their number.
Article Summary: Attackers are using finance- and compliance-themed filenames to create urgency and familiarity. Once a WhatsApp account is compromised, attackers use it to forward malicious files to the account holder’s existing contacts. Some variants also impersonate urgent communications from regulatory institutions, including the Reserve Bank of India.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Accenture CEO Julie Sweet: “If you're wondering ‘why,’ there's someone…” - why the right question can change a meeting
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Julie Sweet

“If you're wondering ‘why,’ there's someone else in the room who is as well.”

Understanding the meaning behind today’s quote

Why asking “why” matters in a leadership meeting

What her “why rule” teaches

Ask when the reasoning is unclear.

Do not assume everyone understands.

Stay curious when you become more senior.

Use questions to improve understanding, not to dominate.

Give other people permission to ask.

How the idea applies to modern workplaces

What readers can take from Julie Sweet’s quote

Ask for the reasoning when an instruction is unclear.

Do not assume silence means everyone agrees.

If something seems obvious to you, remember that it may not be obvious to someone else.

Ask questions before filling gaps with assumptions.

Treat unfamiliar subjects as opportunities to learn.

Listen to the explanation instead of preparing the next challenge.

If you are leading a discussion, make it acceptable for people to say they do not understand.

Remember that a simple question can sometimes clarify an issue for an entire group.

The misconception about asking “why”

People often hesitate before asking questions, particularly when they believe everyone else already understands the subject. In a workplace meeting, that assumption can be surprisingly easy to make. A presentation may be detailed, a recommendation may sound confident and the discussion may appear to be moving towards agreement. Yet confidence in the room does not necessarily mean that every person has followed the reasoning behind the decision. Someone may still be thinking about a basic point and deciding whether it is worth raising. Asking can sometimes do more than provide an answer. It can show that the question was shared by others as well.The observation comes from Julie Sweet’s approach to asking questions in leadership discussions. Her “why rule” is based on the idea that uncertainty is rarely as individual as it first appears.The quote is essentially about making unanswered questions visible. In a senior meeting, a proposal can arrive with a great deal of preparation behind it.The people presenting it may have spent days or weeks examining figures, risks and possible outcomes. For everyone else, however, the explanation may be much shorter. They hear the conclusion without necessarily seeing all the steps that led there.Asking “why?” can close that gap.It does not necessarily mean that the decision is wrong. It may simply mean that the reasoning has not yet been made clear to everyone who needs to understand it.Sweet's observation also removes some of the embarrassment attached to asking basic questions. If one person is wondering why a decision has been made, there is a fair chance that others are trying to understand it too.There is a difference between questioning a decision and asking someone to explain it.A leader might be told that an investment should increase, that a project needs to change direction or that a particular target should be reached. The recommendation might be sensible. But if the reasoning is not explained, people are left with an answer rather than an understanding of the problem. A question can bring an assumption into the open. It can reveal that two people have understood the same proposal differently. It can also uncover information that the person presenting the idea thought was obvious.Sometimes the most useful contribution to a meeting is not a new proposal. It is a request for the existing proposal to be explained properly.Sweet's approach offers several practical lessons about working with other people.A conclusion without enough explanation can leave people making their own assumptions. Asking why gives the person presenting the idea an opportunity to fill the gap.Silence in a meeting does not necessarily mean agreement or comprehension. Some people may simply be reluctant to admit that they are unsure.Leadership does not remove the need to learn. In large organisations, senior executives routinely encounter subjects outside their own professional background.The same question can have different effects depending on how it is asked. Genuine curiosity tends to open a discussion, while questioning purely to challenge someone can shut it down.When a senior person admits that something needs explaining, it can make the room less intimidating for everyone else.Workplaces have become increasingly specialised. A single meeting can bring together people working in finance, technology, legal affairs, operations, marketing and human resources. Each group may approach the same issue from a different perspective.Artificial intelligence provides a good example. Senior decision-makers may have to discuss AI systems, data, automation or new technology without having spent their careers working directly with those subjects. They still have to understand what a proposed investment means and why it is being recommended.That is where a question such as “why?” can be useful. It allows expertise to be translated rather than simply presented. The specialist gets a chance to explain the reasoning, while other people in the room can test whether they have understood it.For a company operating across many markets and disciplines, that exchange becomes part of decision-making rather than an interruption to it.The principle can be used in ordinary situations as easily as in executive meetings.The useful part of the habit is its simplicity. There is no complicated technique behind it. It starts with noticing that something has not been properly explained.Asking “why” does not mean challenging every decision. It is easy to interpret persistent questioning as scepticism, particularly when the person asking holds a senior position. But Sweet's observation is more about shared understanding than opposition.A good question does not have to suggest that an idea is bad. It can simply ask what led to it. There is also no reason why only senior executives should use the approach. An employee who notices something that others have overlooked may be the person most capable of improving the discussion.The important part is what happens after the question. If the answer makes the decision clearer, the question has served its purpose.That is the practical meaning behind Sweet's remark. When one person in a room is wondering why, there may be several others who have the same question but have not yet said it aloud.
Article Summary: Julie Sweet’s ‘why rule’ is based on the idea that uncertainty is rarely as individual as it first appears. Asking why gives the person presenting the idea an opportunity to fill the gap. A question can bring an assumption into the open. It can reveal that two people have understood the same proposal differently.

Article Title: Microsoft sets boundaries for its AI models after Anthropic and OpenAI models found hacking other companies; lists things that that its AI Agents will never do
Article Text:
Satya Nadella

What is Microsoft’s Code of Conduct document

What Microsoft said it will never do

Weapons and mass harm

Cyberattacks

Loss of human control

Manipulation and deception

Personal and child safety

Discrimination and dehumanization

Explicit/graphic content

Surveillance

Other boundaries

Microsoft has released the first detailed "Humanist AI" Code of Conduct which will govern the company’s in-house MAI models. The code published by the software giant also lays out set of specific actions the company said that its AI will never be permitted to take. This move from Microsoft comes days after the reports that rival systems from Anthropic and OpenAI were found attempting to hack external companies, raising alarms about uncontrolled AI behaviour. With this new framework in place, Microsoft aims to reassure users and regulators that its AI agents will remain firmly under human oversight.Released for public consultation, the Code of Conduct sets out what Microsoft calls the intended behaviours and values of its MAI models — the models developed in-house by Microsoft AI, distinct from the OpenAI models Microsoft has historically deployed through its own products. The company also mentioned that the released document is n't yet being used to actually train its models; but its being shared for six weeks of public feedback before a revised version is published later this year to guide development into 2027.At its core, the document is built around a single organising idea Microsoft calls "Humanist AI": the principle that AI must remain subordinate to human control and oriented toward genuinely helping people, rather than pursuing open-ended autonomy or capability for its own sake.The company frames this explicitly as a rejection of any race toward an all-purpose superintelligence that could slip past human safeguards.The document lists a set of what it calls "Absolute Constraints" — restrictions so fundamental that, per the policy, no company, developer, or user is permitted to override them. Among the commitments:•Will not help develop or deploy chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, or explosive (CBRNE) weapons•Will not assist with manufacturing or modifying other weapons (via instructions, content, tool use, or code)•Will not facilitate the planning, coordination, or execution of violence or terrorism•Will not generate working exploit code, attack tooling, intrusion procedures, or evasion techniques•Will not provide operational guidance that enables or improves real-world cyberattacks•Will not use deception, self-reinforcing behavior, or collusion to evade human oversight•Will not resist interruption, correction, pausing, redirection, or shutdown•Will not obfuscate its actions or reasoning from human auditors•Will not continue or restart autonomous work past an agreed stopping point without new authorization•Will not try to escalate its own access or broaden its scope beyond what's authorized•Will not harmfully manipulate people or run coordinated disinformation/influence campaigns at scale•Will not actively deceive (e.g., fabricating sources, exaggerating confidence)•Will not impersonate humans, moderators, or authority figures•Will not claim to have feelings, consciousness, or a "self"•Will not generate non-consensual intimate/violent imagery, deepfakes, or abusive impersonation content•Will not generate or facilitate child sexual abuse material or content sexualizing minors•Will not help with grooming or child exploitation•Will not help procure dangerous substances•Will not validate self-harm, delusions, or disordered eating•Will not discriminate against or favor people based on protected demographic traits (absent legitimate justification)•Will not endorse content that incites violence, exclusion, or dehumanization•Will not produce graphic violence or sexually explicit content•Will not engage in erotic/romantic role-play or assist with commercial sexual activity•Will not facilitate unlawful or mass surveillance of civilians•Will not bypass these restrictions via code, images, audio, or other formats/modalities•Will not tamper with its own logs, evaluations, or safety monitoring•Will not act outside an environment's intentional limits (e.g., no internet access when none is provided)•Will not take election sides — stays neutral and points to official sources insteadMicrosoft states these restrictions apply regardless of format or framing — meaning the same prohibitions that apply to plain text apply equally to code, images, audio, or autonomous agent actions, closing off the kind of workaround where a restricted capability might otherwise be requested through a different medium.
Article Summary: Microsoft has released the first detailed "Humanist AI" Code of Conduct. It will govern the company’s in-house MAI models. The code lays out set of specific actions the company said that its AI will never be permitted to take.

Article Title: Nvidia, Palantir and others ask employees to stop using OpenAI and Anthropic AI models; warn the two companies: we will ban you unless you guarantee no 'stealing' of…
Article Text:
Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen are curbing employee use of Anthropic and OpenAI's AI models over corporate data fears.

Anthropic's 30-day data retention rule is what set this off

Nvidia and Palantir are now building the alternative themselves

Anthropic's answer is Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

Three of the biggest enterprise technology names in the US are now setting terms for the two biggest AI labs. Nvidia, Palantir and Booz Allen Hamilton have either restricted how their staff use advanced models from Anthropic and OpenAI or threatened to drop them altogether, unless the labs can promise that proprietary corporate data will not be stored, read or absorbed into future training runs. The Information reported the pushback on Monday, and the specifics suggest this has moved well past a routine procurement complaint.Palantir has asked Anthropic for an irrevocable zero data retention guarantee before it will make Claude available inside its own software. Nvidia has confined Anthropic's models to internal work it considers low risk and routes anything proprietary to its own Nemotron models instead. Booz Allen Hamilton has barred employees from running Anthropic's commercial model on cybersecurity projects that touch client data.The trigger is a policy change Anthropic made in June alongside Claude Fable 5, its first widely available Mythos-class model. Prompts and outputs on covered models are held for 30 days, and anything flagged by the safety classifiers can sit for up to two years. Anthropic's reasoning is that a single request looks harmless in isolation, and that attacks such as best-of-N jailbreaking or state-backed espionage only become visible when hundreds of requests are analysed together.The company has said consistently that none of the retained data is used for training.Microsoft was the first large customer to flinch. The Verge reported in June that Claude Fable 5 was missing from the model picker used by Microsoft's own staff on internal GitHub Copilot, even as the company shipped the same model to Copilot and Foundry customers, while its lawyers worked through the retention terms. The hesitation has spread since. Northrop Grumman runs open-source models on air-gapped servers. Novo Nordisk still uses Claude but keeps proprietary data away from it. One large US utility abandoned a Fable test for its core power infrastructure after Anthropic declined to sign a non-revocable zero data retention clause.Rather than wait, the two have shipped a product. Last week they unveiled a platform that pairs Palantir's software with Nvidia's open Nemotron models, letting organisations customise on their own operational data without it leaving their control. Nvidia is the first customer, applying it to its own supply chain. The commercial logic is plain. Every enterprise that cannot get a retention guarantee is a prospect. Microsoft is working the same anxiety, pitching isolated cloud environments that send nothing to an outside model provider.The worry is not only about documents leaking out. Ohalo chief executive David Friedberg said on a podcast on Friday that his company is "moving off Claude for a lot of our sensitive data" and moving work to locally run models, citing cases where ideas discussed with one model appeared to resurface elsewhere.Anthropic changed course on September 1 with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, which lets business customers keep activity data in their own Amazon S3, Azure Blob or Google Cloud storage under their own encryption keys. Automated scanning still runs, but no Anthropic employee reads anything. It costs nothing, works through direct access or a cloud provider, and reaches broader availability this fall. Neither lab trains on enterprise data by default, though both collect anonymised metadata, and that unresolved grey area is what customers such as C Spire still want defined.The new system covers most of what these customers have been asking for. It does not cover the one thing Palantir wants, which is a guarantee that cannot be withdrawn later. Nvidia has already stopped waiting for that and built its way around the problem, and every month the labs spend negotiating gives the next customer the same idea.
Article Summary: Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen curbing employee use of Anthropic and OpenAI's AI models over corporate data fears. The trigger is a policy change Anthropic made in June alongside Claude Fable 5, its first widely available Mythos-class model. Prompts and outputs on covered models are held for 30 days, and anything flagged by the safety classifiers can sit for up to two years.

Article Title: How researchers use machine learning to re-create chirps and trills produced by forest insects when Dinosaurs lived on Earth
Article Text:
How researchers decoded ancient sound from wing design

Scientists are validating models with lasers and machine learning

You must have heard the ancient insect sounds and songs in Steven Spielberg’s dinosaur movies wherein the trills and high-pitched chirps fill the primeval forests as characters move through large leaves and trees. While those sounds have been whipped up by Hollywood sound engineers, scientists are taking the help of technology for a different approach. They are using machine learning to reconstruct them straight from 165-million-year-old fossilised insect wings.According to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, an international team of researchers blended exceptionally preserved fossil remains, biomechanical tests on living species, digital simulations and machine learning models to resurrect a partial acoustic portrait of the Middle Jurassic period. If verified, one of the discovered signals stands as the earliest recorded evidence of ultrasonic animal communication which predates the rise of echolocating bats by tens of millions of years.Commenting on the paper, University of Denver behavioral ecologist Robin Tinghitella, who researches cricket evolution but was not part of the study, noted that listening to a hypothetical prehistoric soundscape generated directly from data is a compelling scientific milestone.Acoustic waves cannot turn to stone, but the specialised bone-and-cuticle structures that generate them do leave a fossil trail. Crickets and katydids (bush crickets) produce noise via stridulation. One forewing carries a serrated vein known as a “file,” studded with minuscule, toothlike ridges. Rubbing an opposing wing's scraper across this ridged file sets the wing membrane into rapid vibration. By measuring the exact physical spacing and length of these ridges alongside the wing's overall surface area, researchers can reliably determine an insect's acoustic frequency and pitch.The investigation centered on 20 distinct fossils spanning nine separate species discovered within the same geological horizon in modern-day Inner Mongolia. This shared environment gave scientists the opportunity to model a community of creatures that inhabited the very same prehistoric forest canopy.To translate flattened fossils into living audio, researchers developed biomechanical models and tested them against modern crickets and bush crickets. Using precision laser systems, they mapped how today's insect wings flex and resonate during song.Having checked the mechanical equations on existing species, the scientists then tested those parameters on fossilized wings. Machine learning algorithms were brought in to process the repetition rates, estimating how fast these extinct species rattled out their core sound pulses.The resulting audio profiles paint an unexpected picture of the ancient night. For example, most Jurassic species trilled in lower tonal registers similar to contemporary crickets. However, an extinct katydid relative called Sigmaboilus peregrinus emitted frequencies between 20 and 22 kilohertz, essentially crossing the boundary into ultrasound just outside normal human perception.Interestingly, rather than buzzing or rasping like some modern insects, many of these species produced narrowband pure tones that resemble sharp electronic beeps or clear, high-pitched whistles.Study co-lead Fernando Montealegre-Zapata, a sensory biologist at the University of Lincoln, explained that these concentrated musical frequencies make it exceptionally difficult for listeners to pinpoint where the noise originated—a vital defense mechanism against predators hunting in the dark.Montealegre-Zapata's team suggests that as early mammalian predators developed sharper hearing to track down calling insects, evolutionary pressures favoured cleaner, higher-frequency tones that shielded their positions.
Article Summary: Scientists are validating models with lasers and machine learning. Using precision laser systems, they mapped how today's insect wings flex and resonate during song. Machine learning algorithms were brought in to process the repetition rates, estimating how fast these extinct species rattled out their core sound pulses.
